{{Short description|American mathematician (1935–2021)}}{{Infobox person
| name               = Shirley McBay
| birth_date         = May 4, 1935
| death_date         = November 27, 2021
}}

'''Shirley Ann Mathis McBay''' (May 4, 1935{{snd}}November 27, 2021) was an American mathematician who was the founder and president of the Quality Education for Minorities (QEM) Network, a nonprofit dedicated to improving minority education.<ref name="qemmission">{{Cite web|url= http://www.qem.org/mission/ |title= Our Founder |publisher= Quality Education for Minorities (QEM) Network |access-date= March 5, 2017}}</ref> She was the dean for student affairs at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) from 1980 to 1990.<ref name="tech.mit.edu">{{Cite web|url= http://tech.mit.edu/V110/N17/mcbay.17n.html |title= Dean McBay to step down |last= Rosenberg |first= Brian |date= April 6, 1990 |work= The Tech |access-date= March 5, 2017}}</ref> She was the first African American to receive a Ph.D. from the [[University of Georgia|University of Georgia (UGA)]] (1966, mathematics).<ref>{{Cite book|title= We Shall Not Be Moved: The Desegregation of the University of Georgia |last= Pratt |first= Robert A. |date= 2002 |page= 127 |publisher= University of Georgia Press |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=SlN7iicbHMAC&pg=PA127 |access-date= March 5, 2017|isbn= 9780820326320 }}</ref> McBay was also the first woman of any race to receive a Ph.D. in mathematics from UGA.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Celebrating the Genius of Shirley M. McBay, Ph.D. |journal=Spelman College |url=https://www.spelman.edu/academics/mathematics/shirley-mcbay-tribute.html |access-date=17 August 2025}}</ref> McBay was recognized by [[Mathematically Gifted & Black]] as a [[Black History Month]] 2017 Honoree.<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=Shirley Mathis McBay|url=https://mathematicallygiftedandblack.com/honorees/shirley-mathis-mcbay/|access-date=|website=Mathematically Gifted & Black}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Shirley Ann Mathis was born in [[Bainbridge, Georgia]], on May 4, 1935.<ref name="nytobit" /> She received a B.A. in chemistry from [[Paine College]] in 1954, graduating ''summa cum laude''. While also teaching chemistry at [[Spelman College]], McBay earned an M.S. in chemistry (1957) and M.S. in mathematics (1958) from [[Atlanta University]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/blackwomenscient00warr|title=Black women scientists in the United States|last=Wini.|first=Warren|date=1999|publisher=Indiana University Press|isbn=0253336031|location=Bloomington|oclc=42072097|url-access=registration}}</ref> In 1964, she earned a [[United Negro College Fund|United Negro College Fund Fellowship]], sponsored by the [[IBM Corporation]], that allowed her to study at the [[University of Georgia]] and earn a Ph.D. in mathematics in 1966.<ref>{{Cite web|url= http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/PEEPS/mcbay_shirley_mathis.html |title= Shirley Mathis McBay |last= Williams |first= Scott W. |publisher= The Mathematics Department of The State University of New York at Buffalo |access-date= March 5, 2017}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> Her Ph.D. was advised by Thomas Roy Brahana with a dissertation on ''The Homology Theory of Metabelian Lie Algebras''.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|401}}</ref>

==Career==
McBay spent 15 years at [[Spelman College]] as a faculty member and administrator. McBay's leadership at Spelman led to the creation of the division of natural sciences and an increase in an emphasis on the sciences at the institution.<ref name=":0" /> She served as chairman of the division until 1975 and as associate academic dean at Spelman from 1973 to 1975.<ref name=":0" /> During this time, she created pre-freshman summer programs to increase interest in science majors, which led to the creation of a chemistry department and the renovations of existing science buildings.<ref name=":0" />

She left Spelman in 1975 and took a position at the [[National Science Foundation]] for five years.<ref name="qemmission" /><ref name=":0" /> While at the National Science Foundation, she became program director of the Minority Institutions Science Improvement Program.<ref name=":0" /> She then worked for ten years at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] as the dean for student affairs. Thirty months of this time included being the director of the [https://qem.org/ QEM Project], a study of minority education problems. The QEM Project was the impetus for the [https://qem.org/ Quality Education for Minorities] (QEM) Network that McBay founded and was president of from 1990 to 2016.<ref name="tech.mit.edu" /><ref name="qemmission" />

In December 2021, the University of Georgia's Science Library was renamed the Shirley Mathis McBay Science Library in her honor. <ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.libs.uga.edu/science | title=Shirley Mathis McBay Science Library &#124; UGA Libraries }}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Her husband, chemistry professor [[Henry Cecil McBay|Henry C. McBay]], died in 1995. The couple had married in 1954. McBay died from complications of diabetes on November 27, 2021, in [[Los Angeles]], at the age of 86.<ref name="nytobit">{{Cite news|last=Risen|first=Clay|date=December 14, 2021|title=Shirley McBay, Pioneering Mathematician, Is Dead at 86|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/12/14/science/shirley-mcbay-dead.html|access-date=December 15, 2021|issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Dr. Shirley Ann Mathis McBay |url=https://www.dignitymemorial.com/obituaries/los-angeles-ca/shirley-mcbay-10468556 |website=Dignity Memorial |access-date=2 December 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Shirley McBay obituary |url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/obituaries/article/shirley-mcbay-obituary-p555mg8dr |access-date=17 January 2022 |work=[[The Times]] |date=17 January 2022}}</ref>
